plan.role: You coordinate private events for a restaurant group in Chicago, planning them and running them on the night.
plan.toolWhy: You said writing follow up emails and vendor chasers take up your whole afternoon. ChatGPT is a good place to start because the free version is enough to begin, it works in a browser or a phone app, and you type to it like a text message.

firstWin.prompt: I’m an event coordinator for a restaurant group in Chicago, and I need a follow up email to a vendor for a private event. Event: [event name] on [event date and time]. Guest count: [guest count]. What I need confirmed: [item or service] by [deadline]. Write a short email with a subject line, under 100 words, polite but clear about the deadline. Ask them to reply with a confirmation or any changes. Sign it from [my name].
firstWin.example:
Subject: Confirming [item or service] for [event name]

Hi [vendor first name],

We’re expecting [guest count] guests for [event name] on [event date and time]. Could you confirm [item or service] by [deadline]? If anything has changed, please let me know in your reply so we can adjust in time.

Thank you,
[my name]
fixes: Shorter.
Warmer, like I’m writing to a regular.
Make the deadline more obvious.

ideas.title: Client event recap emails
ideas.why: Turns your event notes into a clear recap without starting from a blank page.
ideas.prompt: I’m an event coordinator for a restaurant group. Write a recap email to a client after their private event. Leave out names. Here are my notes: [what went well, guest count, anything to follow up on]. Keep it warm and professional, under 150 words, with a subject line, and end by inviting them to book again. Sign it from [my name].

ideas.title: Run of show checklists for event nights
ideas.why: Gives you a clear order for the night that you can adjust fast.
ideas.prompt: I run private events for a restaurant group. Make a run of show checklist for an event night. Event type: [event type]. Guest count: [guest count]. Doors at [time], dinner at [time], end at [time]. Include setup, vendor arrivals, guest arrival, service, and breakdown. Put it in a simple list with a time next to each step so I can paste it into Google Sheets.

ideas.title: Post event thank you texts
ideas.why: Gives you a quick, friendly text to send after each event.
ideas.prompt: I’m an event coordinator and I text clients after their private event. Write three short thank you texts I can choose from. Each one should be under 40 words, friendly, and sound like a real person. Leave out names, I’ll add them. The event was a [type of event] and one thing that went well was [detail].

ideas.title: Texting clients
ideas.why: Helps you answer quick client questions in a clear, friendly way.
ideas.prompt: I’m an event coordinator for a restaurant group and I text clients all day. Help me write a short text reply to a client who asked: [paste their question without names or phone numbers]. Here is what I want to say: [my answer]. Keep it friendly, clear, and under 40 words, and make it sound like a text, not an email.

ideas.title: Follow up emails
ideas.why: Gets a polite nudge to clients drafted fast.
ideas.prompt: I’m an event coordinator for a restaurant group in Chicago. Write a follow up email to a client who hasn’t answered about [what I’m waiting on, like final guest count or menu choice]. The event is on [event date]. Leave out names. Keep it friendly but clear about the deadline of [deadline], under 100 words, with a subject line. Sign it from [my name].

ideas.title: Room setup instructions for the team
ideas.why: Turns your plan into steps your setup crew can follow.
ideas.prompt: I plan and run private events for a restaurant group. Turn my notes into clear setup instructions for the team. Room: [room name]. Layout: [seating style and table count]. Special items: [decor, AV, signage]. Setup should be done by [time]. Put it in a short numbered list in plain words that I can text or print.

ideas.title: Event inquiry reply with next steps
ideas.why: Gives you a ready reply to new leads that explains what happens next.
ideas.prompt: I’m an event coordinator for a restaurant group in Chicago. Write a reply to someone asking about a private event. They want [type of event] for about [guest count] guests around [date]. Thank them, ask two or three useful questions, and offer a call at [day and time]. Don’t invent prices or availability. Keep it warm and under 120 words. Sign it from [my name].

ideas.title: Easy meals after late event nights
ideas.why: Gives you simple food ideas for the days when you get home late.
ideas.prompt: I work late on event nights and get home tired. Give me five simple dinner ideas I can make in about the time it takes to unwind, using basic things like [ingredients I usually have]. I don’t eat [foods to avoid]. Include a short shopping list and keep each idea to two or three sentences.

ideas.title: Plan a free weekend in Chicago
ideas.why: Helps you plan a real day off after busy event weeks.
ideas.prompt: I work events and my weekends are often busy, so I want to plan one free weekend well. I’m in Chicago. I like [things I enjoy] and my budget is [amount]. Make a relaxed plan for Saturday and Sunday with a few options for each part of the day. Remind me to check hours and prices myself before I go.

safeUse: Read and check everything before it goes out. You send it, so it is yours.
AI can be confidently wrong about facts, dates and numbers, so check guest counts, times and deadlines against your sheet.
Never type in client names, phone numbers, email addresses or home addresses. Use placeholders like [client] and add real details yourself.
Never type in guest allergy lists tied to names, payment card details or anything about a guest’s health.
Keep contracts, pricing, and confidential company details out of your chats unless your company says it’s okay.
Don’t ask AI to confirm what a vendor agreed to. Check the actual thread or contract.
plan.workProfile: I’m an event coordinator for a restaurant group in Chicago. I plan private events and run them on the night. I write to vendors, clients and my own team, mostly by email, text and Google Sheets. My emails should be short, polite and clear about deadlines. Texts should sound friendly and natural, like a real person wrote them, not formal. I like plain words, no filler and no long intros. When I ask for a draft, give me one clean version first and use square brackets for details I need to fill in. Don’t make up prices, dates or details I haven’t given you.

atWork.askMessage: Hi [manager or IT contact], I’d like to start using an AI chat tool to help with first drafts of my work writing. I’m thinking of vendor follow up emails, client emails, quick text replies, and event checklists. Which AI tools, if any, are approved for work, and what am I allowed to use them for? atWork.aiTalk: I wanted to let you know I’ve started using an AI chat tool to draft things like vendor follow up emails, client messages and event checklists. It gets me a first draft quickly so I’m not rewriting the same chaser all afternoon. I read and check every message myself before it goes out, and I keep client and guest details out of it. If you have any guidance on how you’d like me to use it, I’m happy to follow it.

plan.role: You’re a social media manager at a skincare brand, running TikTok, Instagram and Pinterest.
plan.toolWhy: You said writing captions and chasing creators for their posts take up your week, and the captions are the part you keep rewriting. firstWin.prompt: I’m a social media manager at a skincare brand. Write an Instagram caption for [product name]. Key ingredient: [key ingredient]. What it does for skin: [skin benefit]. One real product detail to mention: [texture, scent or how it feels]. Our brand voice is [playful, calm or expert]. Keep it under 60 words. ideas.title: Creator follow up direct messages
ideas.why: Stops you rewriting the same nudge when a creator goes quiet.
ideas.prompt: I’m a social media manager at a skincare brand. A creator hasn’t sent the post they agreed to make for [product name], and it was due [date]. Write three direct messages I can send over a few days: a friendly check in, a clearer reminder with the deadline, and a last polite nudge. Keep each under 40 words, warm and relaxed. Leave out names.

ideas.title: Caption variations for A B testing
ideas.why: Gives you different angles to test without starting from scratch.
ideas.prompt: I’m a social media manager at a skincare brand. Here is a caption I like for [product name]: [paste caption]. Write four variations to test against each other: one that opens with a question, one that leads with the ingredient, one that is short and punchy, and one that tells a tiny story. Keep our voice [playful, calm or expert] and under 60 words each.

ideas.title: A monthly content calendar outline
ideas.why: Gives you a starting frame to fill in and paste into Google Sheets.
ideas.prompt: I run TikTok, Instagram and Pinterest for a skincare brand. Build a monthly content calendar outline for [month]. Our focus this month is [product or campaign]. Post about [number] times a week on each platform. Make a table with week, platform, content idea and goal, so I can paste it into Google Sheets. Mix education, behind the scenes and creator posts.

ideas.title: Reply comments
ideas.why: Helps your replies sound warm and specific instead of copied.
ideas.prompt: I’m a social media manager at a skincare brand. Write five short, friendly reply options for these kinds of comments: [a question about how to use a product, a compliment, a question about shipping, a complaint about a result]. Our tone is [playful, calm or expert]. Keep each under 25 words. Leave out usernames and don’t promise anything I haven’t told you.

ideas.title: Reviewing analytics
ideas.why: Helps you turn a pile of numbers into a few clear takeaways.
ideas.prompt: I’m a social media manager at a skincare brand. Here is a general description of how our posts did this month, with no private figures: [for example, short videos got more saves, carousels got fewer shares]. Suggest what patterns this might point to, what I could test next, and three questions I should look into in my own analytics. Keep it plain and brief.

ideas.title: Pinterest pin titles and descriptions
ideas.why: Saves you starting from a blank page for every pin.
ideas.prompt: I manage Pinterest for a skincare brand. Write five pin titles and two short descriptions for a pin about [topic or product]. Use natural search words people might type, like [keywords]. Keep titles under 8 words and descriptions under 40 words, in a [calm, helpful or playful] voice. Don’t make medical claims.

ideas.title: A brief to send to creators
ideas.why: A clear brief means fewer back and forth messages with creators.
ideas.prompt: I’m a social media manager at a skincare brand. Write a short creator brief for a post about [product name]. Include the key message, the points they must mention [list], what to avoid [list], the platform [TikTok, Instagram or Pinterest], and the due date [date]. Keep it friendly, easy to skim and under 150 words.

ideas.title: Easy dinners for a busy launch week
ideas.why: Takes the what’s for dinner question off your plate on busy days.
ideas.prompt: I have a busy week at work with a product launch, so I need simple dinners. Suggest five easy dinners that take little effort and use mostly the same ingredients. I like [foods I like] and don’t eat [foods to avoid]. Give me one shopping list I can use for all five.

ideas.title: A screen free weekend plan
ideas.why: Helps you plan a real break after weeks spent looking at feeds.
ideas.prompt: I work on social media all week and want a weekend away from my screens. Plan a relaxed Saturday and Sunday for me. I like [things I enjoy], my budget is [amount], and I’m in [city or area]. Give me a loose plan with a few options for each part of the day, so I can pick what suits my mood.

safeUse: Read and check everything before it goes out. You are the one posting it.
AI can be confidently wrong about facts, dates and numbers, so check them every time.
Check any ingredient or skin benefit claim against your brand’s approved product information before you post.
Never type in creators’ personal details like phone numbers, addresses or payment info.
Leave out customer names, usernames and private messages when you ask for help with replies.
Keep unreleased launches and private sales or analytics figures out of the chat unless your company says that’s okay.
plan.workProfile: I’m a social media manager at a skincare brand, running TikTok, Instagram and Pinterest. I write captions, plan the content calendar, reply to comments, review analytics and message creators about their posts. My audience is skincare fans who like clear, friendly posts, and the creators I work with are busy, so my messages should be polite and quick to read. I like drafts that sound like a real person, with specific product details instead of generic phrases. Keep captions short with a clear hook. Keep messages warm and brief. Don’t make medical claims, and ask me for details you’re missing.

I have in mind drafting captions, planning the content calendar, drafting comment replies and writing follow up messages to creators. Which AI tools are approved for work, and what am I allowed to use them for? Is there anything I should never put into them, like launch details or creator information?

It gives me a quicker starting point, and I still edit everything so it sounds like our brand. I check every product claim and fact myself before anything goes out. I keep private details about creators and customers out of it. I’m happy to share what’s working if it would help the team.

persona.bio: Sales associate at a clothing store in the mall, part time, about 28 hours. intake.role_summary: You own a small women’s clothing boutique with two part timers, handling captions, customer texts, stock orders and shift schedules.

first_win.intro: You said captions take a lot of your time. Here is one you can reuse for any new arrival.

plan.role: You own a small women’s clothing boutique with two part timers, handling captions, customer texts, stock orders and shift schedules.
plan.toolWhy: You said Instagram captions and texting customers about new arrivals take up your time, and ChatGPT is a good place to start on both. The free version is enough to begin, it works in a browser or a phone app, and you type to it like a text message.

firstWin.prompt: I own a small women’s clothing boutique with two part timers. Write 3 Instagram captions for a new arrival: [item name] in [color], sizes [size range]. The shop is open [shop hours]. Keep the tone warm and friendly, like I’m talking to a regular customer, not pushy. Each caption should be 2 to 3 sentences, end with an easy invite to stop by or message us, and include 3 hashtags, one of them #[shop name]. Don’t make up prices, discounts or details I didn’t give you.
firstWin.example:
1. Just in: [item name] in [color]. It’s the kind of piece you’ll reach for again and again. Sizes [size range], come try it on. We’re open [shop hours]. #[shop name] #newarrivals #boutiquestyle

2. Regulars, this one’s for you. [item name] in [color] just landed. Message us if you want your size set aside. #[shop name] #newarrivals #shopsmall
fixes: Shorter.
Warmer, like I’m texting a regular.
Less salesy, more like a friend.

ideas.title: Size guide replies for Instagram DMs
ideas.why: Gives you a friendly reply ready for the size questions that come in again and again.
ideas.prompt: I own a small women’s clothing boutique. Write 3 short, friendly replies I can send when someone asks on Instagram DMs what size to get. Each reply should ask for [the measurements or fit info I need] and mention that I’ll check what we have in stock. Keep each one under 40 words and warm, like I’m chatting with a regular. Don’t invent sizing charts or stock. Leave out customer names.

ideas.title: A text template for restock alerts
ideas.why: One ready message you can reuse whenever a favorite comes back in.
ideas.prompt: I own a small women’s clothing boutique and I text regular customers. Write a short text template I can reuse when a popular item is back in stock. Include blanks for [item name], [color] and [sizes available], and an easy way to reply to hold one. Keep it under 40 words, friendly and personal, with no pressure. Give me 2 versions.

ideas.title: Monthly sale announcement posts
ideas.why: Gets a clear post drafted so you only fill in the details.
ideas.prompt: I own a small women’s clothing boutique. Write an Instagram post announcing [sale details] running [dates]. Make it friendly and clear, 3 to 4 sentences, with a simple invite to visit us during [shop hours] or message us. Add 3 hashtags including #[shop name]. Don’t make up any discounts, items or dates. Use only what I gave you in brackets.

ideas.title: Texts about new arrivals
ideas.why: Helps you send a personal heads up to regulars without starting from scratch.
ideas.prompt: I own a small women’s clothing boutique and I text my regular customers about new arrivals. Write 3 short text messages about [item name] in [color], sizes [size range]. Make them sound like a note from a friend who runs the shop, under 45 words each, with an easy way to reply to hold one. Leave a spot for [customer first name] and don’t invent prices or discounts.

ideas.title: Ordering stock from vendors
ideas.why: Makes your order messages clear so nothing gets missed or misread.
ideas.prompt: I own a small women’s clothing boutique and I order stock from vendors. Write a short, polite message to a vendor placing an order for [items and quantities], asking about [delivery date or availability]. Keep it clear and professional but friendly, under 100 words. Also give me a quick checklist of things to confirm before I send it. Don’t invent prices or terms.

ideas.title: Scheduling part timer shifts
ideas.why: Turns your shift needs into a clear schedule you can share.
ideas.prompt: I own a small women’s clothing boutique with two part timers. Help me make a weekly shift schedule. Our open days and hours are [days and hours]. Part timer 1 can work [availability]. Part timer 2 can work [availability]. I will cover the rest. Show it as a simple table, then write a short friendly text I can send to both of them to share it.

ideas.title: Easy dinners for late closing nights
ideas.why: Gives you simple meal ideas for days you get home tired.
ideas.prompt: I run a small shop and often get home late and tired. Give me 5 easy dinner ideas I can make in about the time it takes to unwind, using simple ingredients. My food preferences are [preferences or things to avoid]. Add a short shopping list for all five and say which ones I can prep ahead on my day off.

ideas.title: Plan a free weekend
ideas.why: Helps you make the most of a rare day off.
ideas.prompt: I own a small shop, so free weekends are rare. Help me plan [one or two days] in [my city] that mix rest and something fun. I like [things I enjoy] and my budget is [amount]. Give me a simple plan by time of day, with a backup idea in case of bad weather. Keep it relaxed, not packed.

safeUse: Read and check everything before it goes out, whether it’s a caption, a text or a vendor message.
AI can be confidently wrong about facts, dates and numbers, so check sizes, prices, stock counts and order quantities yourself.
Never type in customer names, phone numbers, addresses or payment details, including anything from Square or Venmo.
Leave out your part timers’ personal details, like home addresses or private reasons for time off, when you plan shifts.
Don’t share vendor contracts, account numbers or login details in a chat.
Only promise what’s true in the shop. Add real prices, sales and hours yourself.
plan.workProfile: I own a small women’s clothing boutique with two part timers. I write Instagram captions, text regular customers about new arrivals, answer size questions in Instagram DMs, order stock from vendors and schedule shifts. My customers are mostly regulars, so I like a warm, friendly tone, like a note from a friend who runs the shop. Keep captions short, usually 2 to 3 sentences, and texts shorter than that. Never invent prices, discounts, sales or hours. Leave a square bracket for anything you don’t know, and I’ll fill it in. Plain words, please.

plan.role: You’re a beauty advisor at a department store makeup counter, doing client makeovers, restocking and keeping clients coming back through texts and follow ups.
plan.toolWhy: You said texting clients reminders and writing follow up messages take up your time. Claude is a good place to start because the free version is enough to begin, it works in a browser or a phone app, and you type to it like a text message, so you can keep correcting it until it sounds like you.

firstWin.prompt: I’m a beauty advisor at a department store makeup counter. Write a short reminder text to a client about [product or appointment] on [day and time]. It should sound like me texting a regular: warm, relaxed, plain words, no sales pitch. Keep it to two or three sentences. Use [first name] for her name and [my name] for mine. Give me two versions so I can pick the one that sounds most like me.
firstWin.example:
Version 1: Hi [first name], it’s [my name] from the counter. Just a quick reminder about [product or appointment] on [day and time]. Text me here if you need to move it and I’ll find a time that works. See you soon!

Version 2: Hey [first name], [my name] here. Wanted to remind you about [product or appointment] on [day and time]. Any questions before then, just text me!
fixes: Shorter.
Warmer, like I’m texting a regular.
Less salesy, more like a friend.

ideas.title: Follow up messages
ideas.why: Helps you find the right words after a makeover without starting from scratch.
ideas.prompt: I’m a beauty advisor at a makeup counter. Write a short follow up text to a client a few days after her makeover, checking how she’s liking her new look and inviting her to text me with questions. Warm, casual, no pressure to buy. Two or three sentences. Use [first name] and [my name]. Leave out any real names or purchase details. Give me three versions.

ideas.title: Product tip cards for the counter
ideas.why: Turns what you already know into quick tips clients can take home.
ideas.prompt: I’m a beauty advisor at a makeup counter. Help me write a short tip card for clients about how to apply [type of product, like foundation or blush]. Give me three simple steps and one friendly extra tip. Plain words, friendly tone, under 60 words. I’ll check it against what I know and the brand’s own guidance before using it.

ideas.title: Social media captions for makeovers
ideas.why: Gives you a starting point for Instagram so you aren’t staring at a blank box.
ideas.prompt: I’m a beauty advisor posting on Instagram about a makeover look: [describe the look, like soft glam or bold lip]. Write three short captions in a warm, fun voice that sounds like a real person, not an ad. Add a line inviting people to text or message me to book. Keep each under 30 words. No client names.

ideas.title: A checklist for restocking shifts
ideas.why: Gives you one clear list to follow when the counter needs restocking.
ideas.prompt: I’m a beauty advisor and I restock a makeup counter during my shifts. Make a simple checklist I can keep in my Notes app for a restocking shift. Group it by steps like checking testers, refilling supplies, tidying displays and noting what’s running low. Use short lines with a box to tick. I’ll change it to fit [my counter’s routine].

ideas.title: Talking points for a makeover
ideas.why: Helps you plan a friendly flow for each client chat.
ideas.prompt: I’m a beauty advisor about to do a makeover for a client who wants [her goal, like a natural everyday look]. Write a short list of friendly questions I can ask at the start and a few easy ways to explain each step as I go. Keep it relaxed and plain, not pushy, and easy to skim between clients.

ideas.title: Replies to common client questions
ideas.why: Gives you ready words for questions you get again and again.
ideas.prompt: I’m a beauty advisor at a makeup counter. Write short, friendly text replies to these common client questions: [question 1], [question 2], [question 3]. Keep each to two sentences, in a warm voice like I’m texting a regular. Where the answer depends on details I haven’t given, leave a bracket for me to fill in.

ideas.title: Easy dinners after a long shift
ideas.why: Gives you meal ideas for days when you’re tired from being on your feet.
ideas.prompt: I work long shifts on my feet at a store and get home tired. Give me five easy dinner ideas that take little effort and few dishes. I like [foods I like] and I don’t eat [foods to avoid]. For each one, list the main ingredients and the steps in a few short lines.

ideas.title: A plan for a free day off
ideas.why: Helps you make the most of a rare day off without overthinking it.
ideas.prompt: I have a free day off on [day] and I want it to feel restful but still get a few things done. I have about [how long] free. Build me a simple plan that mixes errands, something fun and some rest. Things I need to do: [list]. Things I’d like to do: [list]. Keep it relaxed and flexible.

safeUse: Read and check everything AI writes before it goes out. It should sound like you.
AI can be confidently wrong about facts, dates and numbers, so double check them yourself.
Never type in client names, phone numbers, purchase history or skin concerns. Use brackets instead.
Never type in company information like sales figures, staff schedules or internal plans.
For product details, ingredients or claims, check against your brand’s approved information, not AI.
Your company restricts AI, so keep practice to made up examples on your own device until you’ve asked.
plan.workProfile: I’m a beauty advisor at a department store makeup counter, and part of my pay is commission. I do client makeovers, restock the counter, and keep clients coming back by texting reminders and follow ups. I write mostly to regular clients and new ones I’ve just met. I like drafts that sound like a real person texting, warm, relaxed and friendly, never pushy or salesy. Keep messages short, two or three sentences, in plain words. Don’t use fancy beauty jargon. Give me a couple of options so I can pick the one that sounds most like me, and leave brackets for names, products and times.

atWork.askMessage: Hi [manager’s name], I’d like to ask which AI tools, if any, are approved for us to use at work. I’m thinking of using one to help draft client reminder texts, follow up messages and Instagram captions. I would not enter client names, contact details or any company information. Could you let me know what is allowed and what isn’t? Thank you!
atWork.aiTalk: I wanted to let you know I’ve started practicing with AI to help me find the right words for client texts and follow ups. I use it for first drafts only, and I read and change everything so it sounds like me before anything goes out. I keep client details and company information out of it completely. It helps me spend less time stuck on wording and more time with my clients. I’m happy to show you how I use it.
